newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. calls on Israel to pay $1.7m. for Qana damages.
newsitem.headline: U.N. calls on Israel to pay $1.7m. for Qana damages.

text.p: The General Assembly endorsed a resolution on Friday calling on Israel to pay more than $1.7 million for damage resulting from its shelling of a U.N. base at Qana, in southern Lebanon, last year in which about 100 civilians taking refuge were killed.
Israel rejected the decision, calling it "fundamentally flawed," and said it was not morally or legally bound to pay.

The resolution, dealing with the financing of the U.N. Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), received 127 votes in favour, with the United States and Israel voting against. Russia which, along with the United States, sponsors the Middle East peace process, cast the sole abstention.
The paragraph in the draft dealing with the damages assessment against Israel was put to a separate vote and received 66 votes in favour, with the United States and Israel opposed and 59 abstentions.

The resolution was called up from the Assembly's administrative and budgetary committee, which adopted it on June 7 by a vote of 107 to two (Israel and the United States), with three abstentions (Japan, Russia and Ukraine).
In a separate vote on that occasion, the paragraph dealing with payment of damages by Israel was approved by 58 to two (Israel and the United States) with 52 abstentions.
Japan and Ukraine, which abstained on the overall resolution in the committee, switched in the Assembly and voted in favour. They again abstained on the damages paragraph.

The resolution was originally sponsored by Tanzania on behalf of the the so-called "Group of 77" developing countries -- now with 132 members -- and China. All committee resolutions require endorsement by the Assembly plenary body.

The UNIFIL budget for the 12-month period from July 1, 1997 to June 30, 1998, is more than $126 million, including the sum charged to Israel. The force, established in 1978, comprises some 4,500 troops and 490 civilians. It has a deficit of about $177 million because of unpaid assessments by U.N. members.

A U.N. inquiry last year found that Israel's shelling of the Qana camp during a drive against Hizbollah guerrillas who had fired rockets into northern Israel was unlikely to have been the result of gross technical or procedural errors, though that could not be completely ruled out.

Israel said the camp, in which about 100 sheltering Lebanese civilians were killed and many wounded, was hit accidentally when it shelled nearby positions from which mortar fire had been directed at an Israeli patrol.

Speaking before the Assembly voting, Israeli envoy David Peleg called the resolution "fundamentally flawed." He said singling out one country to bear the costs of damage to a U.N. force was "utterly unprecedented" and could undermine the established method of financing peacekeeping operations.

"The tragic events that took place at Qana...were brought on by a series of violent Hizbollah attacks against northern Israel which, in the absence of any Lebanese effort or action to prevent them, left Israel with no option but a military one," he said. U.N. and Israeli investigations "confirmed separately the activity of terrorist elements close to the UNIFIL battalion headquarters at the time," he added.
"Israel rejects this resolution...in both letter and spirit and is bound by no legal and moral responsibility for reimbursing the amount referred to," Peleg said.
Lebanese Ambassador Samir Moubarak said the outcome was "a victory for the credibility of the United Nations."
